q: Which statement about testicular development and descent is FALSE?
o: AMH falls after mini-puberty, staying low in childhood
The gubernaculum appears at about 7 weeks' gestation
The testis enters the inguinal canal at 20–28 weeks
SRY is the master switch for the testis-determining genes
e: AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone) stays high throughout childhood and falls only at puberty; LH, FSH, inhibin B and testosterone peak in mini-puberty and then stay low. Testis and ovary use separate genetic pathways. Gonocytes, Sertoli and Leydig cells differentiate at 5–9 weeks. Leydig cell testosterone (peak 14–16 weeks) and INSL3 (insulin-like peptide 3, peak 15–17 weeks) are critical for descent; androgens turn the Wolffian ducts into epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts (not the ureter). Descent depends on the gubernaculum (its swelling from the second trimester makes room), the processus vaginalis, genitofemoral nerve innervation and testicular hormones, not the epididymis. Some cryptorchid boys have subtle hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal defects in mini-puberty or low AMH and inhibin B.

q: Which statement about young adults with congenital urological anomalies is FALSE?
o: An elective caesarean section needs a urologist present
An adult congenital urologist must be board certified
Men treated for posterior urethral valves are infertile
Augmented bladders can give false-positive urine pregnancy tests
e: Recent data suggest fertility after posterior urethral valves is likely normal; valve boys do not have dorsal chordee. Augmentation cystoplasty gives a false-positive urine pregnancy test in about 57%. In exstrophy the testes are normal; mild hypospadias does not need lifelong follow-up. Cystoplasty alone is not an absolute indication for caesarean section (vaginal delivery is an obstetric decision); plan elective sections with the urologist present and avoid emergency sections without such expertise. Board certification in urology is the only formal requirement, but carers should be trained in paediatric and adult reconstruction, with psychology in the MDT (multidisciplinary team). Transition means developing a young adult's understanding of and independence in their care; preparation takes years and reduces anxiety, improves engagement and builds trust. A common driver of non-adherence is the 'desire to be normal' (missing clinics, stopping catheterisation). Care models vary by health system. Lifelong care must be proactive: regular renal and bladder checks, sexual function and fertility, pregnancy planning with obstetrics, and collaboration with other specialties.

t: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and other bacterial STIs
q: Which statement about bacterial sexually transmitted infections is FALSE?
o: Up to 75% of women with chlamydia have no symptoms
Donovan bodies on biopsy confirm granuloma inguinale
Clue cells on wet-mount microscopy indicate bacterial vaginosis
LGV is due to Haemophilus ducreyi serovars L1 to L3
e: LGV (lymphogranuloma venereum) is Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3 (H. ducreyi causes chancroid). Its early ulcer is painless and usually gone by presentation; the commonest presentation (heterosexuals) is the secondary stage of tender, usually unilateral, inguinal or femoral nodes. Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the USA (gonorrhoea second), diagnosed by PCR; untreated, 9.5%–27% cause PID (pelvic inflammatory disease), with tubal scarring, ectopic pregnancy, pain and infertility. Women are more likely to be infected and less likely to have symptoms. Gonorrhoea: quinolones abandoned in 2007 and cefixime as first line in 2012; the book gives ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g (or doxycycline). Update: CDC 2020 gives ceftriaxone 500 mg IM alone, adding doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days only if chlamydia is not excluded. Granuloma inguinale: Klebsiella granulomatis, hard to culture; Donovan bodies are intracellular bacteria in macrophages, deep purple on Wright, Giemsa or Leishman stain. Trichomoniasis: strawberry cervix or vulval rash.
b: Donovan bodies; clue cells; strawberry cervix

t: Anatomy of the testis, cord and scrotum
q: Which statement about testicular and scrotal anatomy is FALSE?
o: Sertoli cell tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier
Testicular lymph drains first to external iliac nodes
Scrotal lymphatics drain to the same-side groin only
The testicular artery is wider than the other two combined
e: Testicular lymphatics ascend in the cord to the para-aortic and interaortocaval nodes. The testis measures about 2.5 × 3 × 4 cm (book), volume 15–25 mL. Its coverings, outside in: visceral tunica vaginalis, tunica albuginea (smooth muscle through collagen), tunica vasculosa. Septa create 200–300 lobules of U-shaped seminiferous tubules (about 1 m long), both ends opening via straight tubules into the rete testis, which forms 12–20 efferent ductules into the caput. Interstitium (Leydig cells, mast cells, macrophages, nerves, vessels, lymphatics) is 20%–30% of volume. Three arteries: testicular (ligation may cause atrophy), deferential and cremasteric. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and anterior scrotal skin. Nerves in chronic orchialgia: perivasal, posterior periarterial/lipomatous and intracremasteric complexes. Testis, epididymis, vas and seminal vesicles have autonomic afferent and efferent innervation. Dartos is continuous with Colles, Scarpa and penile dartos fascia. Penile lymphatics cross the midline (unlike scrotal).

q: Which statement about retroperitoneal tumours and surgery is FALSE?
o: Liposarcoma metastases respond well to doxorubicin
Isochromosome 12p points to a germ cell primary
Solitary fibrous tumour carries a NAB2-STAT6 fusion
After bleomycin, keep FiO2 low and restrict fluids
e: Metastatic liposarcoma responds poorly to chemotherapy. It arises from adipocytes, shows chromosome 12q aberrations (MDM2/CDK4 amplification), needs clinical, radiological and histological correlation to diagnose, is treated by resection, recurs locally in up to 40%, and dedifferentiated (non-lipogenic) areas behave aggressively. Solitary fibrous tumour (formerly haemangiopericytoma) can secrete IGF (insulin-like growth factor) causing paraneoplastic hypoglycaemia; radiotherapy improves margin-negative resection. Ganglioneuroblastoma: mostly first decade, can metastasise; N-myc amplification is adverse; MIBG and MRI stage it (the book calls it lethal; prognosis in fact varies by subtype). Cancer of unknown primary is up to 5% of new cancers, mostly adenocarcinoma, and PET-CT is valuable in work-up. Genitofemoral nerve injury on the psoas causes paraesthesia of the anterior thigh and lateral scrotum. Cisterna chyli: posteromedial to the aorta just above the right renal artery. Modern bilateral RPLND template: paracaval, interaortocaval and para-aortic nodes plus the ipsilateral gonadal vessels (suprahilar and interiliac zones omitted). Full vascular control needs division of 6 infrarenal lumbar arteries (3 pairs). Retroperitoneal tumours grow silently to large size; use cross-sectional imaging, markers (germ cell) and FNA or core biopsy, with MDT multimodal planning (testis cancer is the model; sarcoma heterogeneity limits fixed rules).

t: Physiology of ageing and perioperative care
q: Which statement about the older surgical patient is FALSE?
o: Slow gait speed strongly predicts mortality in elders
Spinal anaesthesia lowers mortality versus general
GFR falls by about 10 mL per decade with ageing
Most perioperative deaths in elders are cardiac
e: Mortality and morbidity do not differ between general and regional anaesthesia in the elderly, though postoperative cognitive change is common. Renal blood flow, mass and reserve fall, but serum creatinine stays the same because muscle mass falls; the book prefers Cockcroft-Gault to MDRD for GFR (CKD-EPI is now standard). Reduced ADH (antidiuretic hormone) secretion increases nocturia. Cardiac output and stroke volume fall; pulmonary diffusion surface falls (V/Q mismatch), and pulmonary problems prolong hospital stay. Hepatic and immune function decline; muscle is lost and fat gained; rhabdosphincter striated muscle decreases. Functional assessment (ADL, mobility, cognition) predicts outcome. Geriatric syndromes: frailty, falls, pressure ulcers, polypharmacy, delirium and incontinence. Frailty phenotype: weight loss over 10 lb a year, weak grip, slow gait, low activity, exhaustion. ADT raises fracture risk. Avoid pethidine (Demerol) and long-term nitrofurantoin (lung fibrosis, renal decline); anticholinergics are a leading cause of delirium. α-Blockers reduce preload: with LVH, aortic stenosis or β-blockers get a medical opinion first; tell the eye surgeon (floppy iris syndrome). Screen for elder mistreatment.

q: Which statement about bladder and urethral injury is FALSE?
o: Blunt intraperitoneal rupture is usually a large dome tear
Uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture can be catheter-drained
Pelvic fracture urethral tears usually damage the sphincter
Major straddle injury of the urethra: suprapubic tube first
e: In pelvic fracture the bulbomembranous junction is more vulnerable than the prostatomembranous junction, so the external sphincter is often intact. In children disruption is usually at the bladder neck; in women avulsion is usually proximal, and both urethra and vaginal lacerations should be repaired primarily. Bladder rupture is in about 10% of pelvic fractures, and 90% of ruptures have a pelvic fracture; high mortality is from non-urological injuries. Associated orthopaedic, vaginal, urethral or rectal injury raises complications (abscess, fistula, incontinence) of non-operative care. CT cystography needs retrograde filling with dilute contrast; plain cystography needs a drainage film; most ruptures have gross haematuria. Intraperitoneal tears cause urinary ascites and peritonitis if not repaired promptly. RUG (retrograde urethrography) is the most reliable urethral study, but in penetrating injury without haematuria, meatal blood or voiding symptoms, intraoperative flexible cystoscopy is simplest and most sensitive. Posterior disruption: realignment (higher stricture recurrence) or suprapubic tube with delayed urethroplasty. Open suprapubic placement allows bladder inspection, antegrade realignment and a large-bore midline tube without harming continence or potency. A 2-cm obliterative defect at 3 months: one-stage perineal anastomotic urethroplasty (incontinence under 5%).
s: Ch 133 Genital and lower urinary tract trauma

q: Which statement about the biology of BPH is FALSE?
o: Alpha-1a is the dominant prostatic adrenoceptor
Early periurethral BPH nodules are mostly stromal
BPH mainly reflects enlargement of existing cells
Androgen withdrawal causes prostate cell apoptosis
e: BPH is a true hyperplasia: more epithelial and stromal cells, not larger ones. Androgens are permissive, not the sole cause; they drive proliferation and differentiation and inhibit cell death. DHT is about 10 times more potent than testosterone (book); androgen receptors and DHT stay high with age; type 2 is the main 5α-reductase in BPH. Serum oestrogen rises with age and prostatic oestrogen receptors may contribute. Transition zone proliferation is glandular. Stroma is 40% of the gland, with prominent smooth muscle; autonomic overactivity may add to LUTS. Detrusor trabeculation reflects more collagen. Familial BPH (probably autosomal dominant, larger glands) accounts for about 50% of men having surgery under 60.

q: Which statement about cryptorchidism is FALSE?
o: Cryptorchid testes show an early loss of gonocytes
It raises the risk of testicular germ cell tumour 2–5 times
Most undescended testes (about 80%) are palpable
Paternity after unilateral orchidopexy is near normal
e: Gonocytes disappear late (delayed, not early); other histological changes are fewer Ad (adult dark) spermatogonia, fewer germ cells per tubule and CIS (carcinoma in situ, now GCNIS). Ad counts may predict fertility. Sperm counts are reduced in at least 25% after unilateral and most after bilateral cryptorchidism. Incidence is 1%–4% of term boys; 60%–70% are unilateral and 20% non-palpable. Spontaneous descent happens in the first few months (rare after 6 months), and testes can reascend. Causes: birth weight, gestational age, genetic and environmental factors. Acquired cryptorchidism (commoner with retractile testes) behaves like congenital; examine yearly; at surgery the epididymis is usually normal (anomalies in 11%–31%), while epididymal anomalies and a patent processus are common in congenital cases. Complications: hernia, torsion (from abnormal tunica vaginalis, not the patent processus), infertility, malignancy (not reactive hydrocele). Tumour risk rises with age at surgery and persists, lower, in the contralateral testis; benign tumours such as mature teratoma are not increased; PLAP+ germ cells occur in normal infant testes. Cystic fibrosis causes absent vas, not cryptorchidism. Ectopic sites are perineal, femoral, pubopenile and contralateral scrotal, not perianal.
b: Delayed gonocyte loss; fewer Ad spermatogonia

q: Which statement about genital ulcer disease is FALSE?
o: Benzathine penicillin is used for every stage of syphilis
Chancroid gives a painful, non-indurated, exudative ulcer
Herpes simplex infection is not a reportable disease
Treponemal antibody titres are used to follow therapy
e: Treponemal tests usually stay positive for life and do not show response. Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL, TRUST) track activity and usually become negative after treatment; a fourfold (two-dilution) change, e.g. 1:16 to 1:4, is significant. Chancre: single, painless, indurated, clean, with non-tender nodes; chancroid nodes may suppurate. Stages: primary (acute), secondary (mucocutaneous and constitutional, maculopapular rash), latent (seropositive, no disease: early under 1 year, late beyond), tertiary (cardiovascular, skeletal, CNS). Bicillin C-R (benzathine-procaine mix) and oral penicillin are not acceptable. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (toxins from killed treponemes): headache, myalgia, fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea. Reportable in every US state: syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, chancroid, HIV and AIDS.

t: Anatomy of the prostate, penis and urethra
q: Which statement about prostatic and penile anatomy is FALSE?
o: The glans penis is an expansion of corpus spongiosum
Peripheral zone holds 70% of glands and 70% of cancers
Fossa navicularis is lined by squamous epithelium
A true prostatic capsule is well formed at the apex
e: There is no true capsule at the apex, where glands blend into the striated urethral sphincter (a site of positive margins); elsewhere the capsule is about 0.5 mm thick. The urethra angles about 35° (range 0–90°) at its midpoint, dividing preprostatic and prostatic segments. Periurethral glands (no periglandular smooth muscle, enclosed by the preprostatic sphincter) and the transition zone give rise to BPH. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is thought to be Wolffian-derived; the anterior zone is fibromuscular stroma. The prostate is 70% glandular and 30% fibromuscular. Lymph drains mainly to obturator and internal iliac nodes; penis, scrotum and perineum to superficial and deep inguinal nodes. Squamous epithelium in the fossa keratinises near the meatus. A permeable septum lets the two corpora cavernosa communicate freely.

q: Which statement about urinary incontinence in the elderly is FALSE?
o: Detrusor overactivity is common even in continent elders
Leakage in the elderly is often multifactorial and reversible
Anticholinergics worsen leakage mainly by limiting mobility
Most incontinent elders never tell their doctor about it
e: Anticholinergics can paradoxically worsen leakage through confusion, dry mouth (more drinking, faster filling) and subacute or acute retention (higher PVR lowers effective capacity), not through mobility. Incontinence is never normal, even with dementia; at 90 at least half are continent. Detrusor overactivity is the commonest finding in incontinent and continent nursing-home residents alike (involuntary contractions in 50%–55% of continent elderly), and 40% of incontinence there is from obstruction or stress leakage; DO also accompanies over half of obstruction and about 25% of SUI and may remit when the outlet is fixed. So DO must reproduce the leak before it is called the cause. Treatment can halve leakage even in nursing homes. Patients stay silent from embarrassment, belief it is normal or untreatable. PVR is essential in all; cystoscopy is not routine; prostate size on DRE correlates poorly with obstruction. Behavioural therapy is the cornerstone (bladder retraining, scheduled toileting, prompted voiding); drugs only supplement. On a cholinesterase inhibitor, a helpful antimuscarinic can be continued with cognitive monitoring. Elderly SUI: hypermobility plus some ISD (intrinsic sphincter deficiency); weight loss, posture, pelvic floor exercises, surgery; fluid and voiding adjustment if leakage starts at 150 mL or more (best above 250 mL). Low fluid intake worsens urgency. Pads by severity and need (not menstrual pads). Stroke, poor mobility or cognition and bowel problems all contribute; timed voiding helps.
b: DO common in the continent too

q: Which statement about genital injury is FALSE?
o: Penile fracture is usually ventrolateral where tunica is thin
Penile replantation: microscopic dorsal neurovascular repair
Human penile bites are closed primarily after lavage
Testicular rupture is best salvaged by early exploration
e: Human bites are irrigated, debrided, given antibiotics and left open; dog bites are irrigated, debrided and closed primarily. Penile fracture usually occurs at the base, ventrolaterally. Use a vertical ventral incision over an obvious defect; if the site is unclear or the urethra is injured, use a distal circumcising incision (and circumcise the uncircumcised to avoid oedema). The book says delay up to 7 days does not change outcome; guidelines still advise prompt repair. Replantation: corporal artery anastomosis is not recommended. Skin loss: foreskin flaps cover small distal defects. Testicular rupture: ultrasound shows intratesticular heterogeneity (a tunica defect is seen less often); repair immediately even when extensive, with tunica vaginalis grafts better than synthetic. Haematocele lies between the visceral and parietal tunica vaginalis. Penetrating proximal bulbar injury: immediate spatulated, stented, tension-free, watertight repair with fine absorbable sutures over a Foley catheter.
s: Ch 133 Genital and lower urinary tract trauma

q: Which statement about BPH epidemiology and assessment is FALSE?
o: Histological BPH is found in about 90% of men in their 80s
Prostate size correlates closely with degree of obstruction
Prostate volume correlates usefully with serum PSA
A Qmax under 10 mL/s suggests obstruction is likely
e: Prostate size does not correlate with obstruction, and symptoms, flow and volume do not correlate usefully with each other; symptoms, bother and QoL correlate well. Histological BPH is rare under 30, then rises almost linearly, with strikingly similar prevalence worldwide; prevalence means existing cases per 100,000 at a set date. IPSS: 7 self-administered questions (do not fill it for the patient), 0–35 (mild 0–7, moderate 8–19, severe 20–35), covering voiding and storage but not incontinence; validated in many languages; a 3-point change is noticeable; symptom scores matter more than flow. TRUS volume is reproducible (DRE is not; MRI reads larger); total and transition zone volumes are similar in age-matched white men internationally. Alcohol lowers testosterone, yet heavy drinkers have less BPH surgery and cirrhotics less BPH. α-Sympathomimetic cold remedies worsen LUTS; antidepressants, antihistamines and bronchodilators add 2–3 IPSS points, but only antidepressants lower flow. Qmax falls with age, and bladder fibrosis occurs, in both sexes; many male LUTS are from detrusor dysfunction, not the prostate. Vasectomy has no link; inactivity, obesity and BMI do.

q: Which statement about evaluating and treating an undescended testis is FALSE?
o: Hormone therapy is not recommended to induce descent
Laparoscopic orchidopexy lowers testis injury risk
The processus is usually closed in a vanishing testis
Cord vessels leaving the internal ring mandate exploration
e: Laparoscopic orchidopexy still risks bleeding, infection and testis or cord injury, plus bowel and great-vessel injury. If vessels exit the ring, an intracanalicular testis must be excluded by exploration (atretic vessels may mean a vanishing testis, but the look is subjective). Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy (one- or two-stage) has more atrophy than primary laparoscopic orchidopexy. Laparoscopy is the procedure of choice for the non-palpable testis; imaging rarely helps. Vanishing testis: contralateral hypertrophy and a scrotal nubbin (unilateral); raised FSH and micropenis (bilateral); no testosterone rise after hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) stimulation suggests absent or abnormal testes. Newborn with bilateral non-palpable testes: immediate specialist referral and karyotype for DSD (difference of sex development); assume 46,XX CAH (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) until proven otherwise; avoid circumcision. Retractile vs undescended: careful examination (warm room and hands, legs abducted, sustained traction, testis size); a prior position reported by another doctor is least useful. Observe to 6 months, then orchidopexy (AUA: within the next year, by 18 months). Hormone trials are confounded by retractile testes, initial position, vanishing testes and randomisation.

q: Which statement about viral genital infections is FALSE?
o: Atypical or pigmented warts should be biopsied
Molluscum contagiosum usually settles without treatment
HPV 6 and 11 cause about 90% of anogenital warts
Genital HSV-1 recurs more often than HSV-2 does
e: Genital HSV-2 recurs about 10 times more often (0.23 vs 0.02 per month). The book gives HSV-2 as 90% of genital herpes; HSV-1 (cold sores) causes the rest, and its share is rising. Silent infection is common. HSV is latent in nerve cell bodies and can cause aseptic meningitis and autonomic dysfunction with retention; diagnosis by culture and typing (PCR is now preferred). HPV 16 and 18 are oncogenic (cervical, vulval, vaginal, anal and penile cancer; HPV 16 commonest in penile SCC). The book says over 99% of cervical and 84% of anal cancers are 'associated with HPV 16 or 18'; in fact about 99% of cervical cancers are HPV-related and 16/18 cause about 70%. Biopsy warts that are atypical, pigmented, indurated, fixed or ulcerated. Vaccine: book quadrivalent (6, 11, 16, 18) for both sexes aged 9–26, best before sexual activity; in males it prevents warts and anal cancer (MSM at high risk). Now the 9-valent vaccine is used and licensed to age 45. HIV raises HPV cancer risk. Koilocytic condyloma in a woman: full genital examination including vaginoscopy. Molluscum (crater of molluscum bodies) can be curetted or frozen with liquid nitrogen if treatment is wanted.

t: Retention, nocturia and UTI in older people
q: Which statement about retention, nocturia and UTI in the elderly is FALSE?
o: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in incontinent elders
A suprapubic tube is preferred for a long-term catheter
Desmopressin brings a real risk of hyponatraemia
Retention can occur with DHIC as well as with obstruction
e: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in the elderly does not cause incontinence and needs no treatment; true UTI may present atypically with confusion, agitation, lethargy or anorexia. Retention: underactive detrusor or DHIC (detrusor hyperactivity with impaired contractility), faecal impaction, pain, anticholinergics, sedating antihistamines, decongestants and opiates; decompress for at least a week (longer if PVR is larger). Raised PVR is common; underactive bladder has structural and functional causes and no effective drug. Nocturia once a night is normal in the elderly (book); it is multifactorial, so one treatment rarely suffices; sleep disorders contribute. Peripheral oedema (venous disease, low albumin, heart failure, NSAIDs, nifedipine, glitazones) is mobilised on lying down; manage with compression stockings, a rapid-acting diuretic in late afternoon or changed diuretic timing, and diet. But if the problem is daytime leakage, shifting night excretion to the day will not help. Recurrent UTI in elderly women: vaginal oestrogen (lactobacilli, lower pH) works; systemic oestrogen may cause incontinence; cranberry failed in trials; α-blockers do little in women.

t: BPH: natural history and urinary retention
q: Which statement about the natural history of BPH is FALSE?
o: In BPH drug trials, age is the strongest predictor of AUR
Higher baseline scores need bigger drops to feel better
Longitudinal population studies are least biased
After spontaneous AUR about three quarters have surgery
e: In population studies (e.g. Olmsted County) age is the strongest AUR predictor; in placebo arms of drug trials (older men already diagnosed) serum PSA and prostate volume predict best. Longitudinal population studies are the least biased but slow and costly; watchful-waiting cohorts and placebo arms have enrolment bias. Placebo response is partly regression to the mean and grows with baseline severity; overall a 3-point fall feels like improvement. AUR incidence ranges from under 5 to over 130 per 1000 man-years by population. AUR is a harder, more objective endpoint than surgery, whose rates vary by region and doctor-patient interaction. Spontaneous AUR: 15% recur and three quarters have surgery; precipitated AUR: 9% recur and 26% have surgery. Hydronephrosis is found in 7.6% of men having BPH surgery, a third of whom have renal insufficiency.

q: Which statement about HIV is FALSE?
o: Envelope gp120 binds the CD4 receptor on T lymphocytes
Antiretroviral therapy is advised at any CD4 count
Recent infection in the source raises needlestick risk
Plasma HIV RNA load best predicts disease progression
e: CDC risk factors for occupational transmission are deep injury (OR 15), visible blood on the device (OR 6.2), a device that was in an artery or vein (OR 4.3) and a source dying within 2 months (OR 5.6); recent infection is not one. HIV is a retrovirus with single-stranded RNA, reverse transcribed to DNA and integrated by integrase; it infects T cells and dendritic cells. Envelope precursor gp160 is cleaved into gp120 and gp41. HIV-2 is rare in the developed world and less transmissible and virulent. Diagnosis (book): screening antibody EIA (enzyme immunoassay; rapid result in 30 minutes), confirmed by Western blot, IFA or HIV-1 RNA; the CDC now uses a 4th-generation antigen/antibody test, then a HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay. In the window period (book: up to 3 months) antibodies may be negative, so use a viral load assay. Overt AIDS = low CD4 count; post-treatment RNA nadir predicts outcome; combination therapy delays progression and prolongs survival. The book says therapy does not necessarily make the patient non-infectious; sustained viral suppression prevents sexual transmission (U=U). Other STIs (especially ulcerative: herpes, syphilis, chancroid) raise HIV risk, and HSV increases HIV replication; circumcision lowers risk; test anyone with or at risk of an STI.
b: Needlestick: deep, blood, vessel, terminal source

q: Which statement about the urology of HIV infection is FALSE?
o: Corticosteroids should not be used to treat Kaposi sarcoma
Indinavir stones are radiolucent even on CT scanning
Two APOL1 risk variants greatly raise the risk of HIVAN
HIV raises the risk of prostate cancer about twofold
e: Prostate cancer risk in HIV is no different or lower (RR 0.70); testicular, renal and penile tumours appear increased, along with Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and cervical cancer. Indinavir stones (protease inhibitor) are soluble at acidic pH; lopinavir, atazanavir, amprenavir and nelfinavir cause stones less often; mixed calcium stones can be opaque. HIVAN (HIV-associated nephropathy): glomerular disease presenting with proteinuria; APOL1 G1/G2 variants (African chromosomes, protect against trypanosomes) raise risk 29-fold (50% vs 12% if untreated), with earlier, faster FSGS. Kaposi sarcoma: HHV-8 is essential; raised, firm, purple plaque; protease inhibitors are antiangiogenic; local lesions get radiotherapy, laser, cryotherapy or intralesional chemotherapy. Testicular atrophy is the commonest intrascrotal finding; voiding dysfunction is common in advanced disease. Protease inhibitors and NNRTIs inhibit CYP3A, so start PDE5 inhibitors at the lowest dose.
